questions.question: How many bones does an adult human have?
questions.fact: Babies are born with around 300 bones. Many of them fuse together as they grow.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.fact: An adult's skin weighs around 4 kg and is renewed constantly. You shed millions of skin cells every day.

questions.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?
questions.fact: The heart's two upper chambers are atria and the two lower ones are ventricles.

questions.question: What is the longest bone in the body?
questions.fact: The femur is about a quarter of your height, and it's one of the strongest bones in the body.

questions.question: Where is the smallest bone in the body?
questions.fact: The stirrup bone, or stapes, in the middle ear is only about 3 mm long.

questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
questions.fact: Your heart pumps around 7,000 litres of blood every day.

questions.question: Which organs filter blood and make urine?
questions.fact: Most people have two kidneys, but you can live a normal life with just one.

questions.question: Which organ makes insulin?
questions.fact: Insulin was first used to treat a diabetes patient in 1922, in Canada.

questions.question: What colour is human blood?
questions.fact: Blood is always red. Veins only look blue because of how light passes through skin.

questions.question: How many teeth does an adult usually have, including wisdom teeth?
questions.fact: Wisdom teeth usually appear between 17 and 25, and some people never get them at all.

questions.question: How many baby teeth does a child usually have?
questions.fact: Baby teeth start falling out at around age 6, usually starting with the bottom front ones.

questions.question: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
questions.fact: Enamel is harder than bone, but it can't repair itself, so look after it!

questions.question: Which blood cells carry oxygen?
questions.fact: Red blood cells live for about 120 days, and each one makes a full trip round your body roughly once a minute.

questions.question: Which blood cells fight infections?
questions.fact: You have far fewer white blood cells than red ones: roughly 1 for every 600 or more.

questions.question: What do platelets do?
questions.fact: Platelets rush to a cut and clump together to plug it within minutes.

questions.question: Where in the body is the cornea?
questions.fact: The cornea is one of the few body parts with no blood vessels. It gets oxygen straight from the air.

questions.question: What is the coloured part of the eye called?
questions.fact: Iris patterns are so unique that they can be used like fingerprints to identify people.

questions.question: How many lungs does a person have?
questions.fact: The left lung is a bit smaller than the right, to make room for the heart.

questions.question: Which muscle under the lungs helps you breathe?
questions.fact: Hiccups are caused by sudden, involuntary twitches of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Where is the Achilles tendon?
options: At the back of the ankle
questions.fact: It's named after Achilles, the Greek hero whose heel was his only weak spot.

questions.question: Which vitamin in carrots is good for eyesight?
questions.fact: Vitamin A helps eyesight, but carrots won't give you night vision. That myth is said to have been spread in WWII to hide Britain's radar.

questions.question: What is normal body temperature in Celsius, roughly?
questions.fact: 37 °C is an average. Body temperature changes a little during the day and is usually lowest early in the morning.

questions.question: What is the largest organ inside the body?
questions.fact: The liver can regrow: even after part of it is removed, it can grow back to almost full size.

questions.question: How much blood does an adult have, roughly?
questions.fact: Blood makes up about 7 to 8% of your body weight.

questions.question: What is the scientific name for the kneecap?
questions.fact: Babies are born with kneecaps made of soft cartilage, which slowly turns into bone.

questions.question: Which is the largest part of the brain?
questions.fact: The cerebrum is split into two halves, connected by a thick bundle of nerves.

questions.question: Where is your "funny bone"?
questions.fact: The "funny bone" isn't a bone at all: it's the ulnar nerve, which sits close to the skin at the elbow.

questions.question: Which of the five basic tastes has a Japanese name meaning "savoury"?
questions.fact: Umami was identified in 1908 by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda while studying seaweed broth.

questions.question: How many senses are humans traditionally said to have?
questions.fact: Scientists say we have many more senses than five, including balance, temperature and knowing where our limbs are.

questions.question: What is the pigment that gives skin its colour?
questions.fact: Everyone has roughly the same number of pigment cells. Skin colour depends on how much melanin they make.

questions.question: Which protein are hair and nails made of?
questions.fact: Keratin is the same protein found in animal horns, hooves and feathers.

questions.question: Which small organ stores bile?
questions.fact: You can live without a gallbladder. It's one of the most commonly removed organs.

questions.question: About how long is the small intestine in an adult?
questions.fact: The small intestine is called "small" because it's narrow, not because it's short; it's much longer than the large intestine.

questions.question: What does your heart do about 100,000 times a day?
questions.fact: Over a lifetime, the heart beats more than 2.5 billion times.

questions.question: What type of joint is the hip?
questions.fact: The shoulder is also a ball-and-socket joint, which is why both can move in so many directions.

questions.question: What is the common name for the clavicle?
questions.fact: The collarbone is one of the most commonly broken bones, often from falling onto an outstretched arm.

questions.question: What does "BMI" stand for?
questions.fact: The formula behind BMI was created in the 1830s by Belgian mathematician Adolphe Quetelet. It can't tell muscle from fat.

questions.question: About how much of the human body is water?
questions.fact: Babies are even wetter: about 75% of a newborn's body is water.

questions.question: What is the medical name for the windpipe?
questions.fact: The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage you can feel at the front of your neck.

questions.question: Food travels from the mouth to the stomach through the…
questions.fact: Food doesn't just fall down the oesophagus: muscles squeeze it along, so you can even swallow upside down.

questions.question: Which organ is known as the "voice box"?
questions.fact: The bump called the "Adam's apple" is part of the larynx, usually bigger in men.

questions.question: What are the tiny air sacs in the lungs called?
questions.fact: Your lungs contain hundreds of millions of alveoli. Spread out, they'd cover roughly half a tennis court.

questions.question: What is the largest muscle in the body?
questions.fact: The gluteus maximus keeps you upright and powers climbing stairs and running.

questions.question: How many hours of sleep do adults generally need?
questions.fact: Experts recommend 7 to 9 hours for most adults, and teenagers need even more.

questions.question: What is the outer layer of the skin called?
questions.fact: The epidermis has no blood vessels, which is why a very shallow scratch doesn't bleed.

questions.question: Which sense is most strongly linked to memory?
questions.fact: Smell signals go straight to brain areas linked with memory and emotion, so a scent can bring back old memories instantly.

questions.question: Where are your biceps?
questions.fact: "Biceps" means "two heads" in Latin, because the muscle has two starting points.

questions.question: A doctor who specialises in skin is a…
questions.fact: "Dermatologist" comes from the Greek "derma", meaning skin.

questions.question: A cardiologist treats problems with the…
questions.fact: "Cardio" comes from "kardia", the Greek word for heart.

questions.question: What does a podiatrist look after?
questions.fact: Each foot has 26 bones, so your two feet hold about a quarter of all your bones.

questions.question: What is the most common blood type in the world?
questions.fact: Roughly 4 in 10 people around the world have O positive blood.

questions.question: Which blood type can be given to almost anyone?
questions.fact: O negative donors are called "universal donors" because their red cells can be given to almost anyone.

questions.question: Which bone protects the brain?
questions.fact: The skull is made of over 20 bones fused together. A baby's skull has soft gaps that close over time.

questions.question: The mandible is better known as the…
questions.fact: The lower jaw is the only bone in the skull that can move.

questions.question: Lack of which vitamin causes scurvy?
questions.fact: Sailors used to get scurvy on long voyages. British sailors got the nickname "limeys" from the citrus they ate to prevent it.

questions.question: Hepatitis mainly affects which organ?
questions.fact: The liver does hundreds of jobs, from cleaning the blood to storing energy.

questions.question: About how many times a minute does a person blink?
questions.fact: People blink less when they stare at screens, which is one reason eyes feel dry after a long time on a phone.

questions.question: What happens to your pupils in the dark?
questions.fact: Your pupils can also widen when you look at something or someone you find attractive.

questions.question: Which part of the eye senses light and sends signals to the brain?
questions.fact: The image on your retina is upside down. Your brain flips it the right way up.

questions.question: What causes goosebumps?
questions.fact: Goosebumps are a leftover from our hairy ancestors: raised hair kept animals warm or made them look bigger.

questions.question: What is the scientific name for the shin bone?
questions.fact: The tibia is the second-longest bone in the body, after the femur.
